abstract: The Kovacs effect, characterized by nonlinear, path-dependent structural recovery, is a hallmark of glassy systems. In soft colloidal microgel glasses, the stiffness of the constituent particles governs their deformation, swelling, rearrangement, and response to external stimuli, thereby dictating the path-dependent structural recovery of these jammed non-equilibrium systems. To investigate this influence, microgels of different stiffnesses were synthesized by adjusting the concentration of the polar crosslinker, N, N'-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA). The relaxation of the storage and loss moduli was measured using oscillatory rheology under diverse temperature ramp rates, and cryo-FESEM imaging provided direct visualization of the underlying particle packing. While the rapid adaptability of soft particles and the kinetic arrest of stiff ones suppresses Kovacs asymmetry, intermediate-stiffness particles exhibit moderate thermoresponsivity, traversing distinct energy landscapes on heating and cooling to maximize asymmetry and dissipation. Cryo-FESEM micrographs, displaying gel-like networks in soft particle suspensions, dense packing in stiff particle suspensions, and disordered, compact structures in intermediate-stiffness systems, corroborate these findings. Our results demonstrate that intermediate-stiffness PNIPAM microgels optimize structural recovery, rendering them promising candidates for forming colloidal glasses and establishing Kovacs asymmetry as a robust probe of non-equilibrium dynamics in glassy systems.
authors: Sonali Vasant Kawale, Ranjini Bandyopadhyay
title: Tuning Thermal Memory and Dissipation in Colloidal Glasses via Microgel Particle Stiffness

abstract:
With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C
                    α
                    -only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.
authors: Mina Cullen, Carmen Biancaniello, Katerina Taškova, Vedran Miletić, Alfonso De Simone, Davide Mercadante
title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models

abstract:
Despite the long-held view of
                    Mycobacterium tuberculosis
                    (
                    Mtb
                    ) as a genetically conserved pathogen, many genomic regions remain poorly resolved due to high sequence homology and repetitive content. Using complete genome assemblies generated from long-read sequencing of 151 globally representative clinical isolates, we comprehensively analyzed genome-wide patterns of genetic diversity and evolution across the
                    Mtb
                    genome. Our analysis uncovers pronounced diversity hotspots within paralogous regions (PRs) generated by recurrent gene conversion between homologous genes. In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the
                    Mtb
                    genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. Our analysis identifies over 300 individual gene conversion events (GCEs) distributed throughout the
                    Mtb
                    phylogeny. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host–pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion actively shapes antigenic and virulence-associated diversity in
                    Mtb
                    .
authors: Maximillian G. Marin, Natalia Quinones-Olvera, Hu Jin, Michael A. Harris, Brendan M. Jeffrey, Alex Rosenthal, Kenan C. Murphy, Christopher M. Sassetti, Heng Li, Maha R. Farhat
title: Gene conversion is a key driver of diversity hotspots in Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens and virulence-associated loci

abstract: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. However, the conformational states sampled along the fold-switching pathway have remained elusive because they are transient and unstable. Using multinuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer and relaxation dispersion NMR, combined with chemical shift–based structure determination and protein engineering, we visualized the atomic resolution structure of an “invisible” state of the metamorphic chemokine lymphotactin. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. The stabilization of such hybrid intermediates is likely to have facilitated the evolution of fold-switching and represents a powerful strategy for protein design.
authors: Bodhisatwa Nandi, Ashok Sekhar
title: Structure of a sparsely populated chimeric intermediate that facilitates fold-switching of a metamorphic protein

abstract: Several filamentous biopolymers exhibit unusual polymerization-depolymerization kinetics where continued elongation (shortening) is possible only in an `active' (`inactive') state while occasional random transition (switching) between the active and inactive states takes place. Here, we present a minimal stochastic model capturing only the key features of random elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a generic filament. The structure and/or function of the filament ends when its length hits a critical value during its shortening; the time to reach this critical length can be formulated as a first-passage time (FPT) and for its calculation the critical length is treated as an absorbing boundary. Moreover, the lengths of the filaments that inspire our model are constrained to a finite maximum value $\mathcal{N}$; therefore, in our model we impose a reflecting boundary beyond which the filament cannot grow. We determined the distribution of the FPT and derived its first two moments. We identify a critical point where the drift of the tip of the filament vanishes making its movement purely diffusive; at this critical point, in the limit $\mathcal{N} \to \infty$, the fluctuations in the FPT diverges and MFPT becomes infinite indicating `critical slowing down'. Our analytical results will serve as the testing ground for the accuracy of the approximate theoretical results of more realistic models for polymerization-depolymerization kinetics of specific bio-filaments.
authors: Manvendra Singh, Ashok Garai, Debashish Chowdhury
title: Stochastic model of elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a polymeric filament: Critical slowing down of first-passage and finite-size regularization

abstract: Understanding the behaviour of moving objects within confined granular media is important in many technical applications. In this work we study the vertical pullout of a plate-like intruder buried at different depths within a dense granular aggregate from the onset of motion to flow around the intruder in the steady state by means of a two-dimensional polygonal Discrete Element Method. We find that the peak and steady-state drag forces depend differently on their embedding depth for different friction coefficients. Depending on the strength of friction the plate may interact with the domain walls, which enhances the drag force until failure of the aggregate, but not in the steady-state as dilation around intruder directs the force chains emanating from the plate upwards and away from the walls. If the inter-particle friction is weak, it is possible for the overhead pressure to overcome frictional resistance beyond a certain embedding depth. This prevents the formation of dilated failure zones above the intruder and changes the failure mode of the aggregate, leading to a slower decay of the steady-state drag forces with pullout distance.
authors: Dominik Krengel, Jian Chen, Shun Nomura, Hidenori Takahashi
title: Influence of embedding depth on the pullout of a plate from a confined granular medium

abstract: The human ether-a-go-go-related gene (hERG) potassium channel is an important off-target in drug discovery, as its inhibition can disrupt cardiac repolarisation and cause potentially fatal arrhythmias. Despite its importance, the molecular mechanisms underlying hERG ion permeation and its modulation by small molecules remain elusive. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to reproduce sustained K+ permeation and single-channel conductance comparable to experimental measurements. Our simulations reproduce the characteristic asymmetry in hERG single-channel conductance and reveal a structural mechanism underlying this behaviour. We identify the conformational dynamics of S624, located at the innermost ion-binding site of the selectivity filter, as a determinant of this conductance asymmetry. Substitution of S624 with the canonical threonine abolishes conductance asymmetry by facilitating K+ entry into the S4 binding site. Simulations of classical hERG inhibitors from cryo-EM-derived binding poses show that bound inhibitors sterically occlude K+ access to the selectivity filter, with binding stabilised by interactions with hydrophobic residues lining the central cavity. In contrast, simulations of hERG activators support a fenestration binding mode consistent with mutagenesis data, in which PD-118057 and PD-307243 increase cavity K+ occupancy and enhance conductance by two- to threefold relative to the apo channel. Together, these results establish a molecular framework connecting hERG structure, ion permeation, and small-molecule modulation, providing a basis for directly assessing the functional consequences of compound binding.
authors: Manoza, I.; Gapsys, V.; Kopec, W.
title: Computational assay of hERG ion permeation and its modulation by small-molecule compounds

abstract: Circadian disruption is a known driver of multisystem pathophysiology, yet how it interfaces with the gut microbiome and systemic metabolism across the life course, and how these interactions are shaped by biological sex, remains poorly defined. We performed longitudinal multi-omics characterization of Bmal1-deficient mice in both sexes across three developmental stages. Ablation of Bmal1 induced core circadian disruption phenotypes, including reduced lifespan, decreased body weight, impaired glucose tolerance, and loss of locomotor rhythmicity, and drove sex- and age-dependent metabolic reprogramming, characterized by divergent insulin sensitivity and systemic lipid profiles. Loss of Bmal1 resulted in pronounced, sex- and age-dependent reorganization of gut microbial community structure and rhythmicity, with specific genera (e.g., norank_f_Muribaculaceae, norank_f_norank_o_Clostridia_UCG-014, Bifidobacterium, Allobaculum) exhibiting altered diurnal oscillations and divergent ecological trajectories across aging. Concurrent plasma metabolomic profiling unveiled sex‑specific metabolic variations and time‑of‑day‑dependent differences in circulating metabolites, suggesting coordinated disruption of microbiome-metabolome dynamics. Targeted quantification further revealed sex‑ and age‑specific alterations in plasma short‑chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Tissue‑specific gene expression analysis in the jejunum, colon, and liver revealed sexually dimorphic and age‑dependent transcriptional reprogramming of clock, barrier, inflammatory, and lipid‑metabolism genes, further underscoring the multi‑organ impact of Bmal1 deficiency. Integrated multi-omics correlation analysis demonstrated that associations between gut microbiome, plasma metabolites, and host glycolipid phenotypes are jointly shaped by sex and developmental age. Our findings identify aging and biological sex as pivotal, non-redundant ecological modifiers of circadian-associated host-microbiome interactions, underscoring the necessity of incorporating these variables into mechanistic models and translational strategies for circadian-related disorders.
authors: Yu, Peijun, Liu, Huan, Dong, Zhixiang, Zhou, Wenjing, Liu, Lu, Jin, Qinyang, Chen, Shuai, Huang, Yufei, Yang, Yunpeng
title: Murine circadian disruption modulates gut microbiome and plasma metabolome dynamics in a sex- and age-dependent manner

abstract: Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) is widely used for quantifying molecular dynamics in live cells. However, conventional FCS relies on the autocorrelation function (ACF), a lossy transformation that discards higher-order information, mathematically couples distinct biophysical parameters, and requires long measurements (~50,000 frames, or ~1 minute) that obscure short-lived transient events. To overcome this information bottleneck, we introduce ImFCSViT, a spatiotemporal Vision Transformer-based framework that bypasses the ACF representation entirely, operating directly on raw fluorescence image stacks. By introducing a dedicated normalization token to preserve global intensity statistics, our approach simultaneously extracts four biophysical parameters (diffusion coefficient D, particle density N, particle brightness B, and PSF structure factor {sigma}0) in a single forward pass. Requiring only 2.5 s of data, and potentially down to 1 s (a 1-2 order reduction in data requirement), our approach accurately recovers diffusion coefficients while utilizing its spatial field-of-view to reveal spatially heterogeneous, slow-diffusing sub-populations in lipid bilayers and live-cell plasma membranes that are invisible to classical FCS. By leveraging the data-driven representational learning capabilities of deep learning, we present a flexible, generalizable, and powerful tool for mapping complex, multi-parameter spatiotemporal dynamics in biological systems.
authors: Sim, S. R.; Wang, Z.; Zhou, S.; Pandey, S.; Wohland, T.
title: Vision Transformers as a Framework for Imaging Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy

abstract: The large-conductance calcium-activated potassium (BK) channel plays a critical role in neuronal excitability and spike timing precision. Mammalian BK channels are distinguished by an exceptionally high unitary conductance (~250 pS), while invertebrates exhibit a significantly lower unitary conductance. We confirmed the evolutionary trend to high unitary conductance and used computational models to examine how differences in unitary conductance affect calcium activation of BK channels and influence neuronal dynamics. We show that mammalian BK channels are activated more efficiently by calcium and generate stronger repolarizing currents than lower unitary conductance channels. Channels with lower unitary conductance require greater channel density in the cell membrane, leading to stronger competition for calcium and reduced activation. In contrast, high unitary conductance channels minimize competition, enabling more effective activation and repolarization. Incorporating these channel properties into a neuronal model revealed that mammalian-type BK channels enhance spike-timing precision, consistent with the evolution of fine motor control and advanced neuronal processing in mammals.
authors: Hepburn, Iain, Hellemans, Simon, Taniguchi, Tomohiko, Bourguignon, Thomas, De Schutter, Erik
title: Evolution towards higher unitary conductance in mammals makes BK channels more efficient and precise

abstract: The nucleus is consistently less dense than the surrounding cytoplasm, a difference proposed to arise from selective nuclear import. The functional significance of low nuclear density, however, remains unknown. Because density is a bulk property of the cell, acute perturbations inevitably have pleiotropic consequences. We therefore turned to the natural experiments offered by the tree of life where nuclei vary in genome size, chromatin organisation, import selectivity and transcriptional state, and asked whether low nuclear density is tied to particular nuclear architectures or functions. Using dinoflagellates, Giardia and ciliates, we show nuclear density is uncoupled from genome size. In ciliates, two nuclei in one cytoplasm reach opposite densities relative to it, governed by nuclear import rather than transcription. We thus confirm nuclear import as a major determinant of nuclear density and reveal nuclei that break the low-density rule.
authors: Pleitner, M.; Biswas, A.; Uhlich, J.; Reber, S.
title: The physical state of the nucleus tracks its function across eukaryotes

abstract: MLKL is a key executioner of necroptosis, a lytic form of regulated cell death associated with inflammatory pathologies. Upon activation by RIPK3-mediated phosphorylation, MLKL oligomerizes and translocates to the plasma membrane to induce permeabilization through yet unknown mechanisms. By imaging single particles of MLKL at the plasma membrane of necroptotic cells, here we show that, upon activation, MLKL transitions from a diffuse cytosolic distribution to discrete, low-mobility assemblies before cell bursting. This is accompanied by oligomerization into a mixture of species ranging from monomers up to hexamers. We directly visualize MLKL-induced membrane damage using atomic force microscopy imaging in supported bilayers, which reveals the formation of irregular membrane openings whose edges are only partially decorated with protein. Our findings support a mechanism in which low-order self-assemblies of MLKL disrupt plasma membrane integrity and stabilize membrane defect edges without organizing into defined pore structures, in contrast to membrane permeabilization in other forms of cell death. This reframes necroptosis execution and dissects membrane insertion of MLKL oligomers for potential targeting.
authors: Martinez-Osorio, V.; Zhang, Q.; Zanna, S.; Aufdermauer, J.; Ros, U.; Garcia-Saez, A. J.
title: Low-order MLKL oligomers induce irregular membrane defects in necroptosis

abstract: Nuclear speckles (NS) enhance the expression of NS-associated genes, possibly by elevating local levels of factors involved in multiple steps of gene expression. While dozens of large NS are distributed throughout interchromatin regions, the extent to which NS components dynamically redistribute between NS to adjust to local physiological demands remains unknown. Here, we used live-cell imaging of endogenous NS proteins to identify an interchromatin network of connections that functionally link NS throughout the nucleus. Over timescales ranging from tens of seconds to minutes, NS material is transferred through these curvilinear connections, rather than through isotropic exchange across the NS/nucleoplasm interface followed by diffusion in all directions throughout the nucleoplasm as predicted by current models. Multiphase NS-connecting structures form through the dynamic juxtapositions of multiple NS component phases. Each phase exhibits distinct yet recurrent dynamic patterns, but together, they integrate into a more stable, multiphase, NS-connecting structure in an ATP- and transcription-dependent manner. Our findings reveal the existence of a cellular mechanism that facilitates coordinated inter-NS protein trafficking through multiphase connections.
authors: Kim J, Hernandez Gonzalez GA, Chivukula Venkata N, Copik AJ, Han KY, Belmont AS.
title: Non-random inter-speckle material transfer mediated by dynamic multiphase interchromatin connections.

abstract: Fourier ptychographic microscopy (FPM) enables high resolution imaging across large fields of view, but reconstructed images often exhibit background non-uniformity that interferes with quantitative image analysis. Here, a post-reconstruction background correction approach is presented that identifies specimen-containing regions and corrects only the surrounding background, leaving specimen pixel intensities unchanged. The method was effective across amplitude and phase reconstructions of multiple biological specimen types with no loss in image resolution. The method also improved object detection compared with analysis of the uncorrected image data. FPM background correction reduced residual background non-uniformity to 0.61% with only 0.04% structural error, compared with 6.13% structural error for pseudo flat field correction. These results demonstrate that FPM background correction can support more accurate quantitative analysis of FPM image data while preserving specimen information and image resolution, enabling more reliable segmentation and measurement across large fields of view.

abstract: Giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) are a powerful model system for studying protein dynamics in cell-sized compartments with a precisely tunable physicochemical environment. Here, we apply Single-Molecule Displacement Mapping (SMdM) to quantify how luminal viscosity, ionic strength, membrane lipid composition, and protein surface charge of soluble proteins govern intraluminal single-molecule diffusion. Increasing viscosity led to a predictable decrease in the diffusion coefficient. However, spatially resolved diffusion measurements reveal reduced protein mobility near the membrane, suggesting additional membrane-proximal interactions not captured by particle-based simulations. We observe long-range (~1 um) effects of membrane charge on protein mobility that extend well beyond classical Debye screening, which may reflect shape fluctuations of the GUV membrane. For the membrane-associated protein LactC2, we resolve two distinct diffusing populations within a single vesicle, corresponding to free and membrane-bound states. Our workflow provides a quantitative framework for probing single-protein mobility in vesicle-based synthetic cells. These results advance our understanding of how molecular crowding and transient membrane interactions shape protein diffusion within cell-sized compartments, with possible implications for metabolic organization.

abstract: Lateral fluorination has emerged as a powerful design variable in the design of polar liquid crystals, but its interplay with terminal-group identity remains poorly understood. Here we report a 40-member matrix of biphenyl-ester-phenyl mesogens that independently varies lateral core fluorination and terminal-group identity. Increasing lateral fluorination generally suppresses apolar mesophases and clearing points, however this same change can enable polar nematic phase behaviour in conjunction with suitable terminal units. Graph Fourier analysis of conformer averaged atomic charges shows polar materials occupy a high-frequency region of charge-spectral space, consistent with a bond-scale electrostatic motif. Different terminal units can bias this towards higher or lower frequencies, and in doing so can enable polar order to emerge.

abstract: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.
authors: Guilhem Mariette, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Jean Comtet
title: Dramatic pressure-induced slowdown and the soft glassy rheology of water at 2D material interface

abstract: SAXS/SANS determine the size and structure of particles and macromolecules in solution. However, the conventional low-angle determination of the radius of gyration, Rg, cannot separately resolve its scattering-weighted mean and the width of its distribution. Because the apparent Rg includes a contribution from ensemble variance, the distribution width is required even to recover the mean Rg. Here, we introduce TENOR-SAXS, a method for estimating the scattering-weighted width of an Rg distribution by applying two anisotropic digital smearings to a single 2D scattering image. Comparing the smeared images provides curvature information unavailable from the conventional radial profile. The resulting observables require no explicit model of the native instrumental point-spread function and show only weak sensitivity over the range of native resolutions typical of SAXS measurements examined here. Analytical expressions are derived in the low-angle and narrow-distribution limits for ensembles described by a known or independently constrained single-particle form factor. For verification, we simulated scattering by particles with several form factors and ensembles with different size distributions, all agree well with the analytical theory. To leading order, the principal observable depends on the scattering-weighted mean and variance rather than on the distribution's functional form or higher moments. For simulated data corresponding to feasible synchrotron exposure times for biological samples, the distribution width and, expressed as a fraction of its mean, was recovered with a typical discrepancy of ~0.1, while the scattering-weighted mean Rg was recovered with ~2% relative discrepancy. TENOR-SAXS thus provides a framework for estimating ensemble width from existing 2D scattering data without explicit instrumental desmearing and for correcting the variance contribution to the apparent radius
authors: Uri Steinitz, Mathar Kravikass, Gil Koren, Roy Beck
title: Variable-Resolution Scattering Reveals Ensemble Properties

abstract: Can high-harmonic generation track how microscopic intermolecular interactions give rise to macroscopic order? We address this question in the thermotropic liquid crystal 4-cyano-4'-n-pentylbiphenyl, a model system with a well-defined nematic-to-isotropic transition. Using a temperature-controlled flat jet, we show that polarization-resolved high-harmonic generation driven by mid-infrared strong-field pulses is highly sensitive to liquid-crystal order. In the nematic phase, the harmonic yield forms a four-lobed angular pattern with twofold rotational symmetry and is strongest when the driving-field polarization is perpendicular to the molecular director; this anisotropy vanishes in the isotropic liquid. A tight-binding model parameterized by first-principles calculations attributes this response to intermolecular orbital hybridization in short-range antiparallel molecular arrangements. Temperature-dependent measurements across multiple harmonic orders resolve the same first-order phase transition, with each harmonic order exhibiting a distinct optical sensitivity. A multiscale model combining the microscopic response, Landau-de Gennes orientational correlations and phase matching explains this behaviour through the interplay between orientational correlation lengths and harmonic coherence lengths. High-harmonic generation therefore links local electronic coupling to mesoscopic order and macroscopic propagation, providing an all-optical probe of multiscale organization in soft matter.

title: Tracking multiscale liquid crystal order with high harmonic spectroscopy

abstract: Acoustic levitation enables objects to be suspended and manipulated without physical contact, providing a versatile platform for studying the dynamics of freely suspended matter. Yet levitated objects, from droplets and thin films to particle assemblies, frequently rotate spontaneously, and this axial rotation often remains difficult to predict or control. There is no general understanding of how the shape of a levitated object determines whether it rotates, in which direction, or how its rotation changes with acoustic amplitude. Here, we establish how particle geometry and acoustic amplitude govern spontaneous rotation of acoustically levitated objects. We work with a family of shapes we call ``chiral stars'', within which we systematically vary handedness and number of arms. In a symmetric acoustic field, stars that preserve in-plane mirror symmetry do not rotate, while those that break it spontaneously rotate with a direction set by handedness. Beyond this symmetry requirement, we demonstrate that geometry, as encoded by the number of star arms, couples with acoustic amplitude to produce complex, nonlinear dynamics, including spontaneous reversal of rotation direction. To explain these behaviors, we develop a minimal torque model constrained by independent measurements of rotational drag, which captures the observed responses across all star geometries. We then demonstrate predictive power by designing a ``hybrid star'' with a prescribed amplitude-dependent response and reversal voltage. Our results not only establish how particle geometry and acoustic amplitude combine to govern rotation in acoustically levitated systems, but also reveal unanticipated higher-order couplings with the acoustic field. Beyond explaining spontaneous rotation, they open a route toward programmable rotational dynamics in acoustically levitated matter.

abstract: Particle shape plays a fundamental role in the dynamics and pair interactions of active particles. Yet, experimental measurements of anisotropic active particles are largely lacking. Here, we introduce an experimental system that allows us to observe and measure the effective pair interactions of self-propelled active colloidal polyhedra. We realize such a system by 3D micro-printing quasi- 2D polyhedral colloids with edge number N= 3,4,5,6 and infinity and induce propulsion by partially coating them with an iridium catalytic cap and dispersing them in hydrazine. Despite their different geometries, all shapes exhibit similar single-particle positional dynamics. Stochastic Force Inference reveals predominantly radial, non-reciprocal pair interactions with similar attractive and repulsive regimes for all particle shapes at center-to center distances of about two particle diameters. A minimal plausible phoretic active-Brownian-particle model with a disc shape reproduces the experimentally observed behavior and identifies the physical origins: concentration-dependent slowing down sets their dominant angular symmetry, while the spatial geometry of the chemical coupling and phoretic attraction recover their relative magnitudes and angular dependence. We find that the shape anisotropy present in experiments only modulates the magnitudes and angular dependence of these interactions, and that these variations become more pronounced the stronger the anisotropy. Our results demonstrate the interplay of chemically mediated interactions and particle geometry-induced effects at intermediate interaction distances.

abstract: The coil-to-globule transition is a paradigmatic phenomenon in polymer physics and biophysics, in which polymer chains evolve from swollen to globular conformations upon decreasing solvent quality. At equilibrium, this transition can be rationalized in terms of a thermal blob length that diverges at the so-called $Θ$ condition, marking the crossover from self-avoiding to globular conformations. How activity modifies this conformational transition and affects the fundamental length scales at play remains poorly understood. Here, we address this question for tangentially driven polymers using Brownian dynamics simulations, systematically varying both intrachain attraction strength and activity. We find that polar activity smears out the crossover from swollen to globular conformations. Between self-avoiding and $Θ$ conditions, activity dominates by introducing an emergent folding length scale, which acts as an active blob length. In this regime, we demonstrate that the ratio of thermal to active length scales provides a new scaling variable that leads to a universal master curve for active polymer collapse.

title: Emergent Active-Blob Length Scale Governs the Collapse Transition of Tangentially Driven Polymers

abstract: Respiratory viruses spread within the host through a combination of local expansion and occasional long-range dissemination that seeds new infection foci. We present LEAP (Lotka-Euler Airway Pathogen model), an analytically tractable within-host model that captures this two-scale process. The model takes the form of an age-dependent branching process and yields a closed-form expression for the exponential growth rate during early infection. Using empirical data to parameterize the model, we find that productive dissemination requires only a small number of successful long-range seeding events per infected cell, with distinct values for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. LEAP further predicts that, in these well-adapted viruses, interferon-mediated restriction only weakly affects exponential growth, while remaining decisive for poorly adapted pathogens. More broadly, the model provides a flexible framework for experimentally testable predictions of early infection dynamics.

abstract: The correlation between specific amyloid fibril polymorphs and diseases suggests that characterization of heterogeneity in the aggregation process is key to understanding disease mechanisms. In this work, we use single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to quantitatively characterize dimerization of amyloid β (Aβ), the first step of the aggregation process. We find that dimerization is extremely rare, with a high dissociation constant of >16 mM, yet there are multiple dimer states with distinct FRET efficiencies and stabilities, many of which survive for milliseconds to seconds. The dimer population increases with the increasing ionic strength and decreasing pH, indicating the importance of nonspecific electrostatic interactions in dimer formation. MD simulations with enhanced sampling demonstrate the formation of diverse bound states having a range of FRET efficiencies and flexible N termini, compatible with the experimental observations. There are conformational clusters represented by the formation of three mixed parallel/antiparallel β strands forming Greek key-like motifs and the formation of antiparallel β strands, which may be representative of dimers with longer and shorter lifetimes, respectively, observed in the FRET experiment. This structural and kinetic heterogeneity, resulting from transient interactions, reflects the rugged energy landscape of amyloid formation and may be related to the great diversity of fibrils ultimately formed in the aggregation process.

abstract: Enhanced-sampling methods enable molecular simulations to access configurational regions that are difficult to explore with conventional dynamics, but their efficiency often deteriorates as the number of collective variables (CVs) increases. Here, we introduce an enhanced-sampling framework that couples Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) with parallel restrained molecular dynamics simulations to facilitate exploration of higher-dimensional CV spaces. SVGD collectively transports an ensemble of interacting particles toward a target probability distribution by combining mean forces that guide particles toward low-free-energy regions with kernel-mediated repulsive interactions that maintain particle diversity. We validate the approach using an analytically solvable double-well model, followed by aqueous alanine dipeptide and tripeptide in two- and four-dimensional CV spaces, respectively. In each case, the particle ensemble reproduces the corresponding target distribution, and the reconstructed free-energy surfaces agree closely with analytical or umbrella-sampling references. For alanine dipeptide and tripeptide, CV-SVGD requires substantially less aggregate MD sampling than the corresponding umbrella-sampling reference calculations. These results demonstrate the potential of CV-SVGD as a flexible, parallelizable framework for enhanced sampling in multidimensional CV spaces. We additionally provide an open-source Python implementation to facilitate its adoption.

title: Collective-Variable Stein Variational Gradient Descent for Free Energy Surface Exploration

abstract: Eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC assists in the folding of approximately 10% of the cytosolic proteome through an ATP-driven chamber closure cycle, yet the underlying closure mechanism has remained elusive. Here, using cryo-EM and deep learning analyses, we resolve, at near-atomic resolution, the temporal engagement sequence of the eight distinct subunits during human TRiC ring closure triggered by ATP binding. TRiC closes its chamber through the stepwise extension of an apical helical network among subunits around the ring, coordinated with sequential rotations of the equatorial domains. Each subunit responds differently to ATP, rendering the overall motion asymmetric and ordered. This work delineates the complete structural trajectory of allosteric propagation during ATP-binding-induced, rather than hydrolysis-induced, ring closure, and establishes a mechanistic framework linking ATP-driven conformational dynamics to substrate handling.

abstract: An important underlying requirement for deep learning models is the availability of large datasets, however, in sciences such as chemistry and biology, generating experimental data of sufficient size represents a significant bottleneck. In this work, we probed the extent and nature of limited input data, characterize how several protein language models (pLMs) learned on suboptimal datasets, and investigated augmentation approaches to improve predictive model performance. We found that narrowing the distribution of protein-protein complexes in a limited dataset permits an order-of-magnitude decrease in training dataset size, if a model is only expected to generalize to in-distribution data. Similar results were found in active learning (AL), where both in- and out-of-distribution Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) showed a small but consistent increase upon augmentation of the training set with complexes produced by ESM-3, a generative pLM.

abstract: This paper presents an integrated software package for continuum dielectric studies of the de novo designed calcium channel CalC6.3. The package combines Python scripts for cleaning and repairing the original PDB structure (PDB ID: 9DZW) with PDB2PQR to generate a corre-sponding PQR file containing atomic coordinates, partial charges, and radii. It incorporates the Gaussian Ion Channel Molecular Surface Generation package to construct high-quality triangular molecular surface meshes that preserve the complex channel pore geometry while maintaining suffi-nterface-fitted tetrahedral meshes of a simulation box consisting of protein, membrane, and solvent regions. The integrated software package further integrates the structure-preparation and mesh- size-nite element solver to compute electrostatic potentials and ionic concentrations, streamlining the complete workflow from structure preparation to numerical solution. Numerical experiments for an ionic solution containing Ca2+, Na+ , and Cl-ions show preferential Ca2+ accumulation in the narrow selectivity filter formed by six Glu residues, supporting the experimentally observed calcium selectivity of CalC6.3. They also suggest that a smoother molecular surface mesh can improve the convergence and performance of the finite element solver.

abstract: Due to the high penetration power of X-rays, X-ray imaging techniques have been employed to image cellular architecture. Among these techniques, scanning small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) is a powerful method for investigating ordered structures within cells. With the recent advent of high-brilliance synchrotron sources, nano-focused X-rays and fast scanning modes, scanning SAXS can now provide structural information from hydrated cells in liquid environments in little time. However, the high photon flux results in an increased dose and pronounced radiation damage to the intracellular structures. Therefore, strategies are required to monitor and quantitatively analyze the extent of damage. Here, we present a multimodal approach that employs an on-axis, high-speed, brightfield microscope to monitor cellular damage during scanning. This microscope is integrated into the scanning SAXS setup at ID13 of ESRF and records images in synchrony with SAXS data acquisition. We are able to observe and quantitatively track changes in cellular morphology \textit{in situ} and thereby obtain complementary information to that provided by scanning SAXS measurements. Our approach opens up the potential for a multifaceted investigation of radiation damage to biological cells and other sample types.
authors: Yu, B.; Mendes da Silve, R.; Sinha, M.; Roelleke, U.; Burghammer, M.; Koester, S.
title: In situ radiation damage tracking during scanning small-angle X-ray scattering

abstract: Coral host pigments strongly modify the internal light environment of corals, yet their influence on heat dissipation in coral tissue remains poorly understood. Here, we combined scalar irradiance and temperature microsensor measurements with mechanistic multiphysics modelling to quantify how chromoproteins (CPs) and fluorescent proteins (FPs) regulate light propagation and tissue heating in corals. Measurement-informed simulations of coupled radiative and heat transfer showed that high host pigment concentrations increase broadband scattering while strongly absorbing light within their characteristic spectral bands, reducing light penetration into deeper tissue layers and producing localized energy deposition. Under high symbiont densities, tissue heating was governed by absorption by both symbionts and host pigments, whereas in bleached corals, host pigments became the dominant source of heat generation. Heat generated by CP absorption was concentrated within the epidermis, while symbiont absorption caused deeper heating within the gastrodermis. Unlike CPs, FPs additionally redistributed a fraction of the absorbed photons through lower energy fluorescence emission, increasing scalar irradiance at longer wavelengths and shifting energy deposition deeper into the tissue, thereby enhancing subsurface heating relative to the corresponding non-fluorescent CP scenario. In the model, this pathway changes scalar irradiance and predicted energy deposition relative to the same FP parameterization with fluorescence disabled. The magnitude of this effect varied with FP concentration, spatial organization (granular or diffuse), and symbiont density. Model outputs were supported by surface light and temperature microsensor measurements across sampled coral phenotypes and symbiont densities. Together, our results demonstrate distinct modeled optical pathways for CPs and FPs that regulate not only light propagation but also the spatial distribution of heat generation within coral tissues. By balancing light attenuation, spectral redistribution, and heat generation, host pigmentation is thus likely to influence photoacclimation, bleaching susceptibility, and recovery of the coral-algal symbiosis.
authors: Murthy, S.; Bollati, E.; Salih, A.; Kuhl, M.
title: From Coral Color to Tissue Heating: How Host Pigments Redirect Light Within the Tissue

abstract: Theoretical goal-directed movements follow a unique, stereotyped velocity profile, but continuous movement has no unique optimal solution, so it is unclear whether motor optimization makes continuous movement more stereotyped or more diverse. Previous studies indicated higher information content in the dominant hand, suggesting greater diversity. Because continuous velocity is a composition of overlapping joints movement of varying form, timing and amplitude, comparable to the events that compose spike trains and heartbeat series, we asked whether this diversity appears as a wider multifractal spectrum of velocity. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis to motion-capture velocity of cursive handwriting from right- and left-handed participants writing with both hands; hand dominance is a natural experiment in which task and geometry are fixed while optimization varies. With the dominant hand, spectra were wider, had a lower dominant exponent and were more positively asymmetric in both groups, whereas hands with the same functional role did not differ between groups. A logistic regression on the three spectral features identified the dominant hand with a cross-validated AUC of up to 0.93. Optimized continuous movement is thus not more stereotyped but more diverse: complex, neither stereotyped nor random, with multifractality that tracks hand dominance.
authors: Yago Emanoel Ramos, José Garcia Vivas Miranda
title: Multifractality of human upper-limb velocity tracks motor optimization via hand dominance experiment

abstract: We report results from an experimental investigation on the role of intrinsic curvature in the spontaneous entanglement of elastic rods subjected to controlled tumbling. We examine two distinct entanglement mechanisms, knotting and locking, in a statistical ensemble of straight and helical rods with varying arc length and natural curvature. Our primary finding is that natural curvature exerts a dominant, non-monotonic influence on knotting, with a critical curvature that suppresses knot formation and significantly reduces the probability of knotting relative to equivalent straight rods. In contrast, locking is largely insensitive to curvature and scales primarily with rod length. These results, obtained for the macroscopic experimental system studied here, identify geometric parameters that govern distinct entanglement modes in tumbled elastic rods and may inform entanglement processes in microscopic filamentary systems such as DNA.
authors: Fani Derveni, Javier Sabater, Pedro M. Reis
title: Intrinsic Curvature Controls Spontaneous Entanglement of Elastic Rods

abstract: Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.

abstract: Topological defects in nematic liquid crystals have recently received renewed interest due to their important role in non-equilibrium active materials and developing biological systems. While many studies have focused on simulating defect behaviors in these non-equilibrium situations, there has also been recent progress in our analytical understanding of defect morphology and behavior in a number of complicated regimes, such as intricate boundary conditions, anisotropic elasticity, or the presence of flows. Here, we review the analytical theory of disclination structure and dynamics in two-dimensional nematic liquid crystals, highlighting recent methods and results.

abstract: Soft modes of a shell are one-parameter families of non-trivial deformations that preserve the elastic energy. We identify all soft modes of the soft shells described by the variational theory of put forward by Sonnet and Virga (2025). They are seen to be strictly connected with the Bonnet families, a special class of solutions to the problem posited by Bonnet, who asked whether there exist non-trivial isometries that preserve the mean curvature. Differential geometry deems as equivalent all surfaces in one and the same Bonnet family, but continuum mechanics is interested more specifically in soft deformation modes and the shapes they traverse, as they may describe ways to ignite fluctuations of soft shells that ideally require no energy to be activated. We give a general criterion for the existence of soft modes and a method to construct them based on a cascade of path integrations. We apply both criterion and method to some exemplary cases.
authors: Andre M. Sonnet, Epifanio G. Virga
title: Soft elasticity of soft shells

abstract: We investigate quasi-2D active-passive colloidal mixtures with electric field-mediated non-identical interactions: unlike species attract and like species repel. Mapping the steady states across total area fraction and active particle area fraction identifies the regime of active percolated network formation among active fluid and clustered states. Within the percolated network regime, relaxation speeds up with increasing density, contrary to expectations for dense particulate gels. Particle-resolved dynamics and microstructure link this acceleration to activity-driven rearrangements enabled by asymmetric interactions.

abstract: The properties of colloidal suspensions and granular matter change drastically upon adding a small amount of liquid capable of forming capillary bridges between the solid particles. The attractive forces exerted by these liquid bridges induce the formation of particle aggregates and networks, which radically changes the macroscopic mechanical and rheological behaviour. Predicting these forces across bridge sizes, particle separations and wettability is therefore central to particle-scale modelling of capillary suspensions and wet granular matter. While the Young-Laplace equation governing the properties of the liquid bridges is well known, it lacks a convenient analytical solution. Current simulations therefore employ approximate analytic expressions, typically developed for contact angles below ~40° and bridge volumes below ~2.5% of the solid particle's volume. We compare several frequently used expressions from the literature with numerical solutions of the theoretical capillary forces. An overall good agreement is observed in the aforementioned parameter ranges, while the approximate expressions start to deviate outside their intended domains. We propose accurate and computationally efficient expressions for the capillary force that model this behaviour, for contact angles from 5° to 80° and bridge volumes from $10^{-6}$ to 0.15. We also explore mesoscopic 'fluid-scale' simulations of bridges by Multi-body Dissipative Particle Dynamics (MDPD), to ascertain whether this coarse-grained fluid model faithfully captures the continuum capillary forces. Remarkably, a good agreement is observed even for liquid bridges described by a mere few dozen fluid particles. Together, these results offer two approaches, at different resolution scales, for simulating bridges over a wide range of bridge volumes and contact angles.
authors: Stefano Onofri, Thejas Hulikal Chakrapani, Stefan Luding, Elke Scholten, Ahmed Jarray, Wouter K. den Otter
title: Capillary forces between two identical spherical particles

abstract: The gut microbiota shapes host metabolism, development and immunity, yet how the host regulates its composition in the presence of complex ecological interactions remains poorly understood. Recent experiments that measured T cell reactivity to individual strains in germ-free mice inoculated with a defined microbial community found that T cell recognition across microbial strains is sparse but broad, with a few polyspecific clones recognizing antigens shared across taxonomically diverse strains. Reanalyzing these experiments, we show that these T cell responses are associated with abundance changes of the strains they target. To interpret these findings, we develop a model linking the T cell repertoire to microbial abundances, in which a repertoire is allocated to minimize microbe-driven harm at the cost of maintaining an immune response. The model rationalizes the observed sparsity of gut T cell reactivity and shows that this allocation can emerge from competition between T cells for microbe-derived antigens. Finally, we find that while immune recognition can regulate microbial abundances, ecological interactions between strains may interfere with this mechanism. Together, these results provide a quantitative framework for immune control of gut microbial composition and identify principles governing the organization of T cell repertoires in the gut.
authors: Obinna A. Ukogu, Angelina M. Bilate, Thierry Mora, Aleksandra M. Walczak, Armita Nourmohammad
title: Rational T cell repertoire allocation to control the gut microbiota

abstract: Predicting the dynamics of anisotropic mixtures of different species is a challenging theoretical task. We show that Dynamical Density Functional Theory (DDFT), a theory predicting time evolution of the one-particle-density through a free energy functional, can be simplified to a diffusion equation. To quantify the dynamical relaxation behavior, we deduce corrections to the regular long-time collective diffusion coefficients from the direct correlations between the interacting particles and determine these effective diffusion coefficients analytically for a number of hard-particle systems, including mixtures of hard spheres, as well as isotropic and nematic phases of uniaxial spherocylinders and biaxial spherotriangles. Finally, we discuss how to generalize our approach to systems with positional order and suggest a possible application to predicting relaxation times of orientational order parameters.
authors: Anouar El Moumane, G. H. Philipp Nguyen, Klaus Mecke, Hartmut Löwen, René Wittmann
title: Collective diffusion of anisotropic hard-particle mixtures

abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.
authors: Zumrat Usmanova, Ruobing Bai
title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers

abstract: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.
authors: Joël Mabillard, Frédéric van Wijland, Jean-Baptiste Fournier
title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles

abstract: Models of colliding self-propelled rods are abstractions of many real systems such as gliding bacteria and biofilaments displaced by molecular motors. They have been studied mostly in two space dimensions and shown to display a wealth of different collective regimes with many parameters involved in the ensuing phase diagrams. Continuum-level theories faithful to this phenomenology are largely lacking since coarse-graining models of explicit rods is notoriously difficult. Here we study collections of particles in which the rods geometry is taken into account effectively, by implementing the nematic alignment of their velocities and two types of repulsion. These Vicsek-style models are simple enough to be starting points for systematic coarse-graining. We thus derive hydrodynamic equations that we show to have solutions qualitatively faithful to their particle-level origin.
authors: Elia Bronzo, Hugues Chaté, Benoît Mahault, Alexandre Solon
title: From particles to continuum theories in effective models of self-propelled rods

abstract: Motivated by gaps in our current knowledge of the Vicsek model, we present a major update of its phase diagram in two space dimensions, summarizing comprehensive numerical simulations at length- and timescales never explored before. Our main conclusions are that multiple phase separation scenarios are at play, not just the simple microphase separation put forward in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 114, 068101 (2015)], and that the coexistence phase is subdivided in two. We also map out the region of metastability of the homogeneous Toner-Tu liquid phase.

abstract: The Vicsek model continues to be central in statistical physics studies of active matter, with major recent surprises such as the partial metastability of the famous Toner-Tu flocking phase. Here we report on the diversity of band patterns observed in its coexistence phase --some of them never observed before--, but we also argue that most disappear in the infinite-size limit, leaving nevertheless a different picture than anticipated previously. We finally show that these rather regular, globally ordered band configurations can be destroyed by a localized perturbation: the coexistence phase is also at least partially metastable, and thus must be, asymptotically, a disordered phase made of a variety of chaotically interacting traveling bands.

title: Coexistence phase of the two-dimensional Vicsek model

abstract: In systems with coupled order parameters, the relaxation of existing order can modify subsequent transitions, while cooperation and competition between emerging modes can produce complex phase sequences. We develop a modular Landau analysis that locally relaxes noncritical parent-phase variables to obtain effective one- and two-mode free energies. The resulting coefficients quantify relaxation-induced changes in transition characteristics and mode coupling, including changes in transition order for even-symmetry modes. The resulting modules are assembled successively along parent branches, and the equilibrium phase sequence is selected by comparing the fully relaxed free energies of the admissible branches. We apply the framework to ferroelectric liquid crystals, where orientational, polar, smectic, and tilt orders interact and give rise to multiple competing pathways, using a uniaxial model with longitudinal polarization. We fit the model to the measurements reported by Strachan et al. [Adv. Sci. 12(3), 2409754 (2025)]. A single thermodynamic parameter set reproduces the observed transition temperatures, transition types, and phase sequence, while capturing the main birefringence trend. Smectic layer spacing is reconstructed separately through a fitted observation map based on the calculated equilibrium tilt.
authors: Sisi Guan, Yucen Han, Lei Zhang
title: Modular Landau Analysis of Coupled Phase Transitions: Application to Ferroelectric Liquid Crystals

abstract: Obtaining defect-free single-crystals is of crucial importance in soft matter and materials science, spanning both fundamental interests and practical applications. Active crystals, encompassing diverse dense systems from living organisms to artificial metamaterials, can offer a promising platform for autonomous structural reorganization. We demonstrate that increasing spatiotemporal orientational fluctuations around the mean polarized state can enhance crystallographic order in active crystals. Poly-to-single-crystal transformations in defect-rich, self-aligned active Brownian crystals with coupled translational-rotational dynamics are investigated. We show that long-lived persistence with slow alignment controls the defect-annealing capability. By disentangling activity magnitude from associated timescales, we reveal activity-assisted annealing. Tuning the persistence length enables overcoming thermal energy barriers. Simultaneously adjusting persistence and alignment timescales can tune relaxation from `fast' to `slow', yielding defect-rich and defect-free crystals, respectively. Furthermore, active crystals of point particles are found to exhibit similar defect annealing when flocking is delayed by tuning the timescale of the velocity relaxation towards the polarized state. These findings suggest that the mechanism may extend to a broader class of active crystals. Our results intersect statistical physics of living soft matter with the mechanics of defects and microstructures, proposing a nonequilibrium route towards reconfigurable materials.

title: Tunable annealing of defects in self-aligning active crystals

abstract: Hippocampal neurons not only encode the animal's current position, but also generate sequences representing potential future states and past locations. During goal-directed navigation, the represented location sweeps ahead of the animal's location (online forward replay). After such tasks, during rest, neuronal sequences occurring during sharp-wave ripples replay previously explored trajectories (offline forward replay). Following random foraging, however, neuronal sequences resemble Brownian motion, which does not correlate with behavior (diffusive replay). The mechanisms producing such diverse sequences, and their distinct effects on spatial coding and navigation, remain unclear. Here, we address these questions using a closed-loop model of navigation in a two-dimensional open-field environment based on a spiking neuronal network. In our framework, neuronal sequences are generated by a common mechanism driven by background noise and the balance of excitation and inhibition. Different replay modes arise solely from task-dependent synaptic modifications and serve different functions: online forward replay facilitates shortcut discovery, offline forward replay consolidates optimal sequences of actions, and diffusive replay helps in generalizing the action and state map and homogenizing internal connectivity. Together, these results show that a single network architecture can flexibly generate various replay types and clarify how each contributes to optimizing goal-directed navigation behavior.

title: Online Preplay and Offline Replay Optimize Action Selection in a Closed-Loop Navigation Model

abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks

abstract: Mean First Passage Time (MFPT) is a crucial quantity that characterizes stochastic processes in various stochastic dynamical systems across different disciplines. The inverse of the MFPT, known as the escape rate, is helpful in the context of Brownian motion and chemical processes. The MFPT dynamics of a passive particle in the presence of active noises presents a fascinating avenue. In this work, we study the dynamics of two different systems: first, a single Brownian particle and second, a dimer (two Brownian particles connected by a spring). In both cases, the systems are kept in contact with a thermal bath and an active bath, and are trapped in a bistable potential. The active bath produces kicks that follow the Poisson distribution. The MFPT of the particle and the dimer is investigated in various scenarios. Analytical results are presented for the small kick variance approximation only. In this approximation, we formulate the MFPT in two scaling regimes: a weak-noise regime characterized by classical Arrhenius scaling for escape rate and a strong-noise regime in which the MFPT scales as a power law in the effective noise strength. For the general case, the problem is solved numerically. Next, under the same approximation, the MFPT of a dimer in the small-bond-strength regime is studied using a sequential-hopping mechanism, and in the large-bond-strength regime, the MFPT is formulated using the adiabatic elimination approach. Motivated by recent studies on speeding up the escape mechanism, the MFPT of the particle and the dimer in the presence of an intermediate barrier is also examined. We deduced from the numerical results that the MFPT can be enhanced and further optimized by selecting a suitable intermediate potential profile.

title: Poisson-shot-noise induced escape dynamics of a passive particle and a dimer

abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy

abstract: We investigate whether cyclically varying the class composition of training batches can modify both the performance and the internal organization of neural networks. Motivated by nonequilibrium systems, in which cycling between related sub-goals can make switching between their solutions increasingly efficient, we introduce Dynamical Batching (DB), a sampling protocol that periodically emphasizes each class while leaving the loss and the optimizer unchanged, and compare it with Uniform Batching (UB), in which every mini-batch has equal class proportions. In the regime where standard training fails, DB changes the outcome: on a three-arm spiral, a capacity-limited MLP that plateaus far below perfect accuracy under UB fits the training data under DB. Tracking individual weights, we find that under DB the change between class-specialized states is carried by a smaller set of weights than under UB, and that this set is markedly more persistent from cycle to cycle, on every synthetic dataset we test and in a wider network that fits the data under both protocols. This organization is a signature of the protocol rather than a predictor of its benefit: it appears equally where DB leaves accuracy unchanged. On CIFAR-10, the same protocol modestly improves the test accuracy of a channel-narrowed ResNet-10, a standard residual architecture, and of a second capacity-limited convolutional network. These results show that how class emphasis is distributed in time can shape both the solution a network reaches and the internal structure of the network.

title: Dynamical Batching: How Class-Cycling Training Shapes the Internal Structure of Neural Networks

abstract: Our experiments demonstrate the strong stabilizing effect of a viscoelastic shell on flow-focused viscous jets. The results suggest that stabilization occurs when the polymer viscosity, $η_p$, exceeds a critical threshold, provided the extensional relaxation time, $λ$, is large enough to allow the polymer molecules to undergo the coil-stretch transition. Under these conditions, substantial extensional viscoelastic stresses develop as the liquid accelerates. Since both $η_p$ and $λ$ increase with shell viscosity, the polymer concentration required to stabilize the viscous jet decreases accordingly. Remarkably, moderately to highly viscous jets can be stabilized with very small polymer concentrations, for which no beads-on-a-string (BOAS) instability is observed.

abstract: Fiberboids are filaments that self-propel by rolling along a surface due to a flux normal to that surface. In the last few years, fibers using several materials and driving mechanisms have been developed that are able to roll persistently. Here we show using thermally driven nylon fibers on a slightly curved glass surface, that fiberboids also come in another state, that we call ``twitching'': the fiber rolls for a short time and then switches direction, implementing on large scales a diffusion-like motion. We rationalize the occurrence of this effect and experimentally quantify this new dynamic state. We then analyze ensembles of twitching fiberboids and by confining the fibers inside a circular arena to allow them to roll on a single axis only, we implement a simple, table-top realization of a one-dimensional non-equilibrium active gas. We study experimentally active cluster formation, their non-equilibrium dynamics and we rationalize the observations by a simple lattice model. This model takes into account a Viscek-like alignment of the velocity directions of the individual particles within clusters to yield good qualitative agreement with the experiments. Overall our work opens the path to study collectives of self-rolling fibers as an interesting new class of active matter.

abstract: The measurement of guided wave propagation is an effective approach for evaluating arterial wall stiffness. A more comprehensive characterization of viscoelastic material properties could yield more informative biomarkers; however, this additionally requires estimation of wave attenuation. Furthermore, spatially local estimation is necessary for localized pathologies, such as atherosclerotic plaques. To this end, we propose an original two-stage high-resolution method to recover local viscoelastic properties from guided waves in artery-like soft tubes. First, the local frequency-wavenumber dispersion relation including losses is estimated using a high-resolution complex wavenumber identification method. Second, assuming a fractional Kelvin-Voigt rheological model for the tube wall, we estimate the viscoelastic material parameters by fitting the dispersion relation computed with a spectral element method to this estimate. We experimentally validate the proposed approach on flexural wave propagation along water-filled soft tubes, measured with a high-speed camera coupled with digital image correlation. Owing to the high resolution of the method, the axial modulus variation of a graded phantom is recovered. Finally, a Cramér-Rao analysis indicates that the complex wavenumber estimator operates near its theoretical limit, and reveals why local attenuation is intrinsically difficult to recover.

abstract: We examine the known polymorphs of cytidine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate (CMP) using dispersion-corrected density functional theory. The monoclinic phase is predicted to be the most stable, lying 1.76 and 3.00 kcal/mol per molecular unit below the orthorhombic and triclinic forms, respectively. Monoclinic CMP contains a ribose-based H-bonding motif along the crystallographic $\vec{b}$ direction, comprising alternating intra- and intermolecular interactions, motivating an investigation of cooperative stabilization along this pathway. We employ chain-of-molecules (COM) and chain-of-slabs (COS) models to quantify the direction- and size-dependent stabilization and extend the analysis to the corresponding 5$^\prime$-monophosphates of thymidine, uridine, adenosine, and guanosine. Successive dimer-addition energies reveal the strongest size-dependent cooperative stabilization along the $\vec{b}$ direction, whereas growth along $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ exhibits substantially weaker size dependence. Among the nucleotides examined, adenosine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate shows the strongest chain-growth stabilization in the COM model, whereas the uridine variant shows the strongest stabilization in the COS model. Guanosine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate exhibits the weakest response in both models. Minimal-basis iterative stockholder (MBIS) analysis further supports molecular polarization along the growing assemblies. These results demonstrate how nucleobase identity and the surrounding crystal environment modulate direction-dependent cooperative stabilization associated with extended hydrogen-bond networks.

abstract: We construct a hydrodynamic theory of the effect of chiral and active force densities on three-dimensional uniaxial solids. We show that in a fixed background medium active chiral force densities---that arise at lower order in gradients than odd elasticity---generically destabilise the solid state. We further show this active instability also affects isotropic chiral solids in an anisotropic medium, a situation that is relevant for cell clusters moving through the extracellular matrix. Interestingly, the instability is eliminated in a higher-symmetry solid, known as the polar elastomer; indeed, we show that chirality does not affect the leading-order mechanics of such materials. We further demonstrate that momentum-conserving polar active solids have two chiral odd elasticities in contrast to the one discussed for two-dimensional solids. However, we again find that the higher symmetry of polar elastomers eliminates one of these with the remaining one being equivalent to the two-dimensional odd elastic force density. Our results should apply to numerous biological and condensed matter systems.
